decks.title: Goods and Services Tax — Part 1: CGST, SGST, IGST and the bill
goals: Calculate the GST on an article at a given rate
Split the GST on an intra-state sale into equal CGST and SGST
Use IGST for a sale from one state to another
Find the amount a consumer pays after a discount and GST

slides.heading: Goods and Services Tax, Part 1: reading the bill
slides.body_md: Every bill you pay in a shop has a tax line. This chapter explains it.

nodes.label: Price of the article (after any discount)
Add GST at the given rate
The seller passes the GST to the government

visual.alt: Flow of a sale under GST: the price of the article after any discount, then GST at the given rate is added, giving the amount on the bill; the seller passes the GST on to the government.
visual.caption: GST is added to the price; the buyer pays it and the seller hands it over.

slides.narration: Welcome to the chapter on goods and services tax. Look at any shop bill in India and you will see a tax line under the price. In this part you will learn how that tax is calculated, why it is often split into two equal parts, and how a discount changes the bill. The picture shows the journey: price, plus tax, gives the amount, and the tax reaches the government.

slides.heading: What you will be able to do
bullets: Calculate **GST** on a price at a given rate
Split it into **CGST** and **SGST** for a sale within a state
Use **IGST** for a sale between states
Read a **tax invoice** with several items
Find the **amount paid** after a discount and GST
slides.narration: Here are the goals for part one. You will calculate the tax on a price, split it into the central and state parts, and use the integrated tax when goods cross a state border. You will read a tax invoice with several items, and finally combine a discount with the tax to find what a customer really pays.

slides.heading: What is GST?
slides.body_md: The **Goods and Services Tax** is one tax on the supply of goods and services across India, in force since 1 July 2017. It replaced many separate taxes such as excise duty, VAT and service tax.
bullets: Charged on **every sale** in a chain, from maker to shop to customer
Charged on **services** too: repairs, catering, hall rent, software
Paid by the **buyer**, collected by the **seller**, passed to the **government**

visual.alt: Flow of a supply chain: manufacturer to wholesaler to retailer to consumer, with GST charged on each sale.
visual.caption: GST is charged at every sale in the chain, not only at the shop counter.

slides.narration: The goods and services tax is a single tax on the supply of goods and services, in force across India since the first of July, twenty seventeen. It replaced a tangle of older taxes. It is charged at every sale, from the maker to the wholesaler, the retailer and the customer, and on services such as repairs and catering. The buyer pays it, the seller collects it, and the government receives it.

slides.heading: Rates of GST
slides.body_md: Each item has a rate fixed by the **GST Council** (the Union and state finance ministers together). Rates are revised from time to time, so **every problem states the rate to use**. This chapter uses 5%, 12%, 18% and 28%.

visual.alt: Table of GST rates used in this chapter: 5 percent splits into 2.5 percent CGST and 2.5 percent SGST; 12 percent into 6 and 6; 18 percent into 9 and 9; 28 percent into 14 and 14. For an inter-state sale the whole rate is IGST.
visual.caption: Within a state the rate is halved; across states it is charged whole as IGST.

slides.narration: Each kind of goods or service has its own rate, fixed by the council of the Union and state finance ministers, and these rates are revised from time to time. So never try to remember the rate for an item: every problem tells you the rate to use. In this chapter you will meet five, twelve, eighteen and twenty eight percent. The table also shows the halves we are about to meet.

slides.heading: Within a state or across states?
slides.body_md: The **place of the seller and the buyer** decides how the tax appears on the bill.

rows: Nagpur to Pune, both in Maharashtra
CGST + SGST, half the rate each
Centre, which shares it with the state where the goods are used

visual.alt: Table comparing intra-state and inter-state sales: within one state, such as Nagpur to Pune, the bill shows CGST and SGST at half the rate each; between states, such as Coimbatore to Palakkad, it shows IGST at the full rate, collected by the Centre and shared with the destination state.
visual.caption: Where the buyer is decides the heads of tax, not the rate.

slides.narration: Here is the key distinction. If the seller and buyer are in the same state, the sale is intra-state, and the bill shows central tax and state tax, each at half the rate. If the goods go from one state to another, the sale is inter-state, and the bill shows integrated tax at the full rate. The rate itself does not change; only the heads of tax change.

slides.heading: The formulas
bullets: The **price** here is the taxable value: the price after any discount, before tax

nodes.label: Price of the article (after any discount)
Add GST at the given rate
The seller passes the GST to the government

visual.alt: Flow of a sale under GST: the price of the article after any discount, then GST at the given rate is added, giving the amount on the bill; the seller passes the GST on to the government.
visual.caption: GST is added to the price; the buyer pays it and the seller hands it over.

slides.narration: Three formulas do almost all the work. The tax is the rate over one hundred times the price. Within a state, the central and state parts are each half of it. Between states, the integrated tax is the whole of it. And the amount on the bill is the price plus the tax. Remember that the price means the value after any discount, but before tax.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: a sale within Maharashtra
slides.body_md: A furniture shop in Nagpur sells a study table for ₹6,400 to a customer in Nagpur. GST is 12%. Find the CGST, the SGST and the amount of the bill.
bullets: **Step 2 —** Intra-state: CGST $= \text{SGST} = \dfrac{768}{2} = 384$ (each at $6\%$)

visual.alt: Tax invoice line for a study table sold in Nagpur: price 6,400 rupees, CGST at 6 percent 384 rupees, SGST at 6 percent 384 rupees, amount 7,168 rupees.
visual.caption: GST $= 12\% \text{ of } 6400 = 768$, split equally.

slides.narration: First find the full tax: twelve percent of six thousand four hundred is seven hundred and sixty eight rupees. Both people are in Nagpur, so the sale is within Maharashtra and the tax splits equally: three hundred and eighty four rupees of central tax and the same of state tax, each at six percent. Add both to the price. The bill is seven thousand one hundred and sixty eight rupees.

slides.heading: Quick check: the central rate
slides.body_md: A geyser is sold within one city at a GST rate of 12%. At what rate is CGST charged?
slides.narration: Both buyer and seller are in the same city, so the sale is within one state. What happens to the twelve percent? Decide, then choose.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: crossing a state border
slides.body_md: A pump maker in Coimbatore (Tamil Nadu) sells a pump priced at ₹15,500 to a farmer in Palakkad (Kerala). GST is 18%. Write the tax on the bill. What if the farmer were in Tiruppur (Tamil Nadu)?
bullets: Inter-state: IGST $= \dfrac{18}{100} \times 15500 = 2790$; amount ₹18,290
Intra-state: CGST $= \text{SGST} = 9\% \text{ of } 15500 = 1395$; amount ₹18,290
The farmer pays the same either way

visual.alt: Table for a pump priced 15,500 rupees at 18 percent GST: sold to Palakkad in Kerala the bill shows IGST of 2,790 rupees; sold within Tamil Nadu it shows CGST 1,395 and SGST 1,395 rupees. The amount is 18,290 rupees either way.
visual.caption: Same rate and same total; only the heads of tax change.

slides.narration: Coimbatore is in Tamil Nadu and Palakkad is in Kerala, so the pump crosses a state border and the whole eighteen percent is charged as integrated tax: two thousand seven hundred and ninety rupees. If the farmer were in Tiruppur, inside Tamil Nadu, the same amount would be split into one thousand three hundred and ninety five rupees of central tax and the same of state tax. The farmer pays eighteen thousand two hundred and ninety rupees either way.

slides.heading: Reading a tax invoice
slides.body_md: A registered seller must give a **tax invoice**. These are the lines you use in sums.

rows: GSTIN of the seller (and of a registered buyer)
Description and HSN code of each item
what is sold; the code fixes its GST rate
price after any discount, before tax
rate and amount of each tax

visual.alt: Table listing the parts of a tax invoice: the GST identification numbers of the seller and a registered buyer, the description and HSN code of each item, the taxable value, the rate and amount of CGST and SGST or IGST, and the invoice value.
visual.caption: Every GST sum in this chapter is a line of such an invoice.

slides.narration: A registered seller gives a tax invoice. It shows the identification number of the seller, a description and a code for each item, the taxable value, the rate and amount of each tax, and the invoice value. In examination sums you mostly need the taxable value, the tax lines and the total, but it helps to know what the rest of the invoice means.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: several items, several rates
slides.body_md: A stationery shop in Bhubaneswar bills a local student for the items below. Find the total GST, the CGST, the SGST and the invoice value.
bullets: Tax **each line at its own rate**, then add
CGST $= \text{SGST} = 158.50$; invoice value $= 2450 + 317 = 2767$

visual.alt: Invoice table of a Bhubaneswar stationery shop: school bag 1,200 rupees at 12 percent, GST 144; scientific calculator 850 rupees at 18 percent, GST 153; pack of notebooks 400 rupees at 5 percent, GST 20. Totals: price 2,450, GST 317, CGST 158.50, SGST 158.50.
visual.caption: Invoice value $= 2450 + 317 = 2767$ rupees.

slides.narration: When the items have different rates, tax each line separately. Twelve percent of the bag is one hundred and forty four rupees, eighteen percent of the calculator is one hundred and fifty three, and five percent of the notebooks is twenty. The total tax is three hundred and seventeen rupees, split into one hundred and fifty eight rupees fifty paise each. The invoice value is two thousand seven hundred and sixty seven rupees.

slides.heading: Quick check: equal halves
slides.body_md: True or false: on a sale within a state, central GST and state GST are each charged at half the GST rate.
slides.narration: Think about the rate table you saw earlier. Is the split always equal, whatever the rate? Decide, and give a reason.

slides.heading: List price, discount and GST
slides.body_md: Shops often show a **list (marked) price** and offer a **discount**. GST is charged on the **selling price**, the price after the discount.

nodes.label: Plus GST on the selling price

visual.alt: Flow for a discounted sale: list price, minus the discount, gives the selling price, which is the taxable value; GST is added on the selling price to give the amount paid.
visual.caption: Discount first, then tax on what is left.

slides.narration: Many shops show a list price, also called the marked price, and offer a discount. The tax is not charged on the list price. It is charged on the selling price, the value after the discount. So the order is always the same: take off the discount first, then add the tax on what is left. The flow shows the steps.

slides.heading: Worked example 4: discount, then GST
slides.body_md: A refrigerator is listed at ₹24,000. A shop in Lucknow gives a discount of 15% and charges GST at 18% to a local customer. Find the CGST and the amount paid.
bullets: **Step 1 —** Discount $= \dfrac{15}{100} \times 24000 = 3600$; selling price $= 20400$
**Step 2 —** GST $= \dfrac{18}{100} \times 20400 = 3672$; CGST $= \text{SGST} = 1836$

visual.alt: Bar chart for a refrigerator: list price 24 thousand rupees, price after a 15 percent discount 20.4 thousand, GST at 18 percent 3.672 thousand, and amount paid 24.072 thousand rupees.
visual.caption: The amount paid ends up just above the list price.

slides.narration: First the discount: fifteen percent of twenty four thousand is three thousand six hundred, so the selling price is twenty thousand four hundred rupees. Now the tax on that: eighteen percent is three thousand six hundred and seventy two rupees, which is one thousand eight hundred and thirty six of each kind. The customer pays twenty four thousand and seventy two rupees, just a little above the list price.

slides.heading: A common mistake: taxing the list price
slides.body_md: Fifteen percent off and then $18\%$ GST is **not** "$3\%$ more". The multiplier is $0.85 \times 1.18 = 1.003$. Taxing the list price uses $1.18$ and overcharges.

visual.alt: Graph of amount paid against list price. The steep line, 1.18 times the list price, is the wrong method of taxing the list price; the lower line, 1.003 times the list price, is the right method of taking 15 percent off and then adding 18 percent GST. At a list price of 24 thousand rupees the lines give 28.32 and 24.072 thousand rupees.
visual.caption: Taxing the list price would overcharge by more than four thousand rupees here.

slides.narration: Here is a mistake to avoid. Some students add the tax to the list price. The steep line shows that wrong method. The correct method multiplies the list price by nought point eight five and then by one point one eight, which is one point nought nought three. Also notice that fifteen off and eighteen on is not simply three percent more; the multiplier is only slightly above one.

slides.heading: Quick check: half of eighteen
slides.body_md: For a sale within one state at a GST rate of 18%, what is the rate of CGST?
slides.narration: Fill in the blank with a number. Remember how the rate is shared when the buyer and seller are in the same state.

slides.heading: Worked example 5: one jacket, two bills
slides.body_md: A woollen jacket is listed at ₹3,600 with a discount of 15%. GST is 12%. Find the bill for a buyer in Srinagar when the seller is (i) in Srinagar; (ii) in Ludhiana (Punjab).
bullets: (i) CGST $= \text{SGST} = 183.60$; (ii) IGST $= 367.20$
Amount ₹3,427.20 in both cases

rows: Seller in Ludhiana, buyer in Srinagar

visual.alt: Table for a woollen jacket listed at 3,600 rupees with 15 percent off: selling price 3,060 rupees; within Srinagar CGST 183.60 and SGST 183.60 rupees; from Ludhiana in Punjab to Srinagar IGST 367.20 rupees. The amount is 3,427.20 rupees in both cases.
visual.caption: Discount and tax are the same; the heads of tax depend on the states.

slides.narration: The discount gives a selling price of three thousand and sixty rupees, and twelve percent of that is three hundred and sixty seven rupees twenty paise. If the seller is also in Srinagar, it splits into one hundred and eighty three rupees sixty paise of each kind. If the seller is in Ludhiana, the jacket crosses a state border and the whole amount is integrated tax. The buyer pays the same total.

slides.heading: Quick check: a helmet in Vadodara
slides.body_md: A helmet set priced at ₹3,850 is sold within Vadodara at a GST rate of 28%. Find the CGST in rupees.
slides.narration: First decide the central rate from twenty eight percent. Then take that percentage of the price. Type the number of rupees.

slides.heading: Summary of Part 1
bullets: GST is a rate per cent of the price after discount
Within a state: CGST = SGST = half the GST
Between states: IGST at the full rate
Several items: tax each line at its own rate, then add
Discount first, then GST on the selling price

rows: GST on the price after discount

visual.alt: Summary table of part one: GST is the rate over 100 times the price; within a state CGST and SGST are each half the GST; between states IGST is the whole GST; the amount is price plus GST; with a discount, GST is charged on the reduced price.
visual.caption: Part 1 on one card.

slides.narration: To sum up part one. The tax is a percentage of the price after any discount. Within a state it splits equally into central and state tax. Between states it is charged whole as integrated tax. On a bill with several items, tax each line at its own rate. And with a discount, always reduce the price first and then add the tax.

slides.heading: Exam tips for Part 1
bullets: Write "intra-state" or "inter-state" before you calculate
Show the GST, then the split: CGST and SGST each at **half the rate**
Never tax the list price when a discount is given
Keep paise: ₹158.50, not ₹158 or ₹159
State the final answer in rupees with a sentence
slides.narration: Some tips for the examination. Before calculating, write whether the sale is within a state or between states; that decides the heads of tax. Show the full tax first and then the split, because each step carries a mark. Never charge tax on the list price when a discount is offered. Keep the paise exactly as they come. And finish with a clear sentence giving the answer in rupees.

decks.title: Goods and Services Tax — Part 2: Input tax credit, the supply chain and reverse problems
goals: Find the GST each dealer pays using input tax credit
Combine GST with profit, loss, marked price and discount
Show that the total tax to the government equals the tax paid by the consumer
Work backwards to find a price, a rate of GST, a list price or a rate of discount

slides.heading: Goods and Services Tax, Part 2: who pays what
slides.body_md: Tax is collected at every sale, yet the consumer bears it all.

visual.alt: Flow of a mixer-grinder through a chain at 18 percent GST: manufacturer sells for 3,000 rupees and pays 540; wholesaler sells for 3,600 and pays 108; retailer sells for 4,200 and pays 108; the consumer bears 756 rupees of tax.
visual.caption: $540 + 108 + 108 = 756$: the payments add up to the consumer's tax.

slides.narration: Welcome to part two. Goods usually pass through several hands before they reach you: a maker, a wholesaler, a retailer. Tax is charged at every sale. So who actually pays what? In this part you will see how each dealer pays only on its own value added, why the total equals the tax on the last sale, and how to work backwards from a bill.

slides.heading: What you will be able to do
bullets: Use **input tax credit** to find each dealer's **net GST**
Split each payment into **CGST** and **SGST**, or **IGST**
Combine GST with **profit, loss, marked price and discount**
Find a **price, rate, list price or discount** from the amount paid
slides.narration: Here are the goals for part two. You will use input tax credit to find the net tax each dealer pays, and split it into central and state parts, or integrated tax across states. You will mix the tax with profit, loss and discounts. And you will solve reverse problems, finding a price or a rate from the amount paid.

slides.heading: Input tax, output tax and input tax credit
slides.body_md: A dealer **pays** GST when it buys (input tax) and **collects** GST when it sells (output tax). It hands over only the difference.
bullets: The deduction of input tax is called **input tax credit (ITC)**
Within a state, CGST credit is used against CGST and SGST credit against SGST

nodes.label: GST paid on purchases: input tax
GST collected on sales: output tax
Net GST payable = output tax − input tax

visual.alt: Flow showing input tax credit: the GST a dealer paid on purchases, called input tax, is set off against the GST it collected on sales, called output tax; the dealer pays only the difference.
visual.caption: Input tax credit: pay only the difference.

slides.narration: When a dealer buys stock, it pays tax to its supplier. This is called input tax. When it sells, it collects tax from its customer. This is called output tax. The dealer does not hand over the whole output tax; it subtracts the input tax it has already paid. This deduction is called input tax credit, and the dealer pays only the difference.

slides.heading: Why input tax credit matters
slides.body_md: Without the credit, tax would be charged on tax at every stage.

headers: Tax if each sale were taxed in full (₹)
Tax actually paid with input tax credit (₹)

visual.alt: Table comparing a chain with and without input tax credit at 18 percent: without credit the manufacturer, wholesaler and retailer would pay 540, 648 and 756 rupees, total 1,944; with credit they pay 540, 108 and 108, total 756.
visual.caption: Without input tax credit, tax would be charged on tax (a cascade).

slides.narration: Imagine there were no credit. Every dealer would pay tax on its full selling price, and the price at each stage would already include the earlier taxes. In this chain the total would be one thousand nine hundred and forty four rupees instead of seven hundred and fifty six. This piling up is called a cascade. Input tax credit removes it, so each stage pays only on the value it adds.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: a chain within Gujarat
slides.body_md: A mixer-grinder is sold by a maker in Surat to a wholesaler in Vadodara for ₹3,000, then to a retailer in Rajkot for ₹3,600, then to a customer in Rajkot for ₹4,200. GST is 18%. Find the GST each dealer pays, as CGST and SGST.
bullets: Maker: output $540$, no input: pays ₹540
Each payment splits equally: ₹270, ₹54, ₹54 of CGST

visual.alt: Table of the Gujarat chain at 18 percent: manufacturer sells for 3,000, output tax 540, no input tax, pays 540 as 270 CGST and 270 SGST; wholesaler sells for 3,600, output 648, input 540, pays 108 as 54 and 54; retailer sells for 4,200, output 756, input 648, pays 108 as 54 and 54.
visual.caption: Each row: output tax minus input tax, then halve.

slides.narration: Work stage by stage. The maker has no input tax, so it pays the full eighteen percent of three thousand, five hundred and forty rupees. The wholesaler collects six hundred and forty eight and has already paid five hundred and forty, so it pays one hundred and eight. The retailer collects seven hundred and fifty six and pays one hundred and eight. Every payment splits into equal central and state halves.

slides.heading: The payments add up to the consumer's tax
slides.body_md: $540 + 108 + 108 = 756 = 18\% \text{ of } 4200$: the government receives exactly the tax on the last sale.

visual.alt: Bar chart: the manufacturer pays 540 rupees, the wholesaler 108 and the retailer 108; the fourth bar, the consumer tax of 756 rupees, equals the three payments stacked together.
visual.caption: The first three bars add up to the fourth.

slides.narration: Now add the three payments: five hundred and forty, one hundred and eight and one hundred and eight make seven hundred and fifty six rupees. That is exactly eighteen percent of the final price of four thousand two hundred, the tax the customer pays. The dealers only collect and pass on tax; the consumer bears all of it.

slides.heading: Quick check: net GST
slides.body_md: A dealer collected ₹1,440 of GST on sales and had paid ₹1,080 of GST on purchases of the same goods. How much does the dealer pay the government?
slides.narration: Which amount is the output tax and which is the input tax? Decide what the dealer actually hands over, then choose.

slides.heading: A shortcut for one rate
slides.body_md: When the rate is the same on buying and selling:
bullets: The dealer pays GST only on its **margin** (value added)
Profit or loss is worked out on prices **before** tax: GST is not the dealer's money
At a loss the net figure is negative: nothing to pay, the rest stays as credit

headers: Tax if each sale were taxed in full (₹)
Tax actually paid with input tax credit (₹)

visual.alt: Table comparing a chain with and without input tax credit at 18 percent: without credit the manufacturer, wholesaler and retailer would pay 540, 648 and 756 rupees, total 1,944; with credit they pay 540, 108 and 108, total 756.
visual.caption: Without input tax credit, tax would be charged on tax (a cascade).

slides.narration: If the rate is the same when the dealer buys and sells, the net tax is the rate times the selling price minus the rate times the cost price, which is the rate times the margin. So a dealer pays tax only on the value it adds. Profit and loss are always worked out on prices before tax, because the tax is not the dealer’s own money. At a loss, nothing is payable.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: marked price, discount and GST
slides.body_md: A music shop in Kolkata buys a harmonium for ₹5,000 (before GST at 12%). It marks the harmonium 20% above cost, gives a local customer 10% off and charges GST at 12%. Find the GST the shop pays, as CGST and SGST, the amount the customer pays and the shop's profit percent.
bullets: Marked price $= 5000 \times 1.2 = 6000$; selling price $= 6000 \times 0.9 = 5400$
Output $= 648$, input $= 600$, net $= 48$: CGST ₹24 and SGST ₹24
Customer pays ₹6,048; profit $= \dfrac{400}{5000} \times 100 = 8\%$

visual.alt: Flow for a harmonium: cost 5,000 rupees, marked 20 percent higher at 6,000, sold after a 10 percent discount at 5,400, and the customer pays 6,048 rupees after 12 percent GST.
visual.caption: Net GST $= 648 - 600 = 48$ rupees.

slides.narration: Mark up first: twenty percent above five thousand is six thousand. Ten percent off gives a selling price of five thousand four hundred. The shop collects twelve percent of that, six hundred and forty eight rupees, and has already paid six hundred, so it pays forty eight: twenty four of each kind. The customer pays six thousand and forty eight, and the shop’s profit is eight percent.

slides.heading: When a link crosses a state border
slides.body_md: On an **inter-state** sale the dealer charges **IGST**. Its input CGST and SGST are both set off against that IGST.

visual.alt: Table for woollen blankets at 12 percent: the Ludhiana maker sells to a Ludhiana distributor for 40,000 rupees with CGST 2,400 and SGST 2,400; the distributor sells to a Jaipur retailer for 46,000 rupees with IGST 5,520, sets off the 4,800 rupees of input tax and pays 720 rupees of IGST.
visual.caption: Input CGST and SGST can both be used against output IGST.

slides.narration: Sometimes one link of the chain crosses a state border. Then the seller charges integrated tax on that sale. Any central and state tax it paid on its purchase can be set off against this integrated tax, so it pays only the difference, as integrated tax. The table shows an example from Punjab to Rajasthan.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: Ludhiana to Jaipur
slides.body_md: A blanket maker in Ludhiana sells a lot to a distributor in Ludhiana for ₹40,000. The distributor sells it to a retailer in Jaipur (Rajasthan) for ₹46,000. GST is 12%. Find the tax the distributor pays to the government.
bullets: Purchase (intra-state): CGST $= \text{SGST} = 6\% \text{ of } 40000 = 2400$; input tax ₹4,800
Sale (inter-state): IGST $= \dfrac{12}{100} \times 46000 = 5520$
IGST payable $= 5520 - 4800 = 720$

visual.alt: Table for woollen blankets at 12 percent: the Ludhiana maker sells to a Ludhiana distributor for 40,000 rupees with CGST 2,400 and SGST 2,400; the distributor sells to a Jaipur retailer for 46,000 rupees with IGST 5,520, sets off the 4,800 rupees of input tax and pays 720 rupees of IGST.
visual.caption: Input CGST and SGST can both be used against output IGST.

slides.narration: The distributor’s purchase is inside Punjab, so it pays central and state tax of two thousand four hundred rupees each, four thousand eight hundred in all. Its sale goes to Rajasthan, so it charges integrated tax of twelve percent on forty six thousand, five thousand five hundred and twenty rupees. Setting off the input tax, it pays seven hundred and twenty rupees of integrated tax.

slides.heading: Quick check: tax on the margin
slides.body_md: True or false: when the GST rate is the same on its purchase and its sale, a retailer's net GST payable equals that rate applied to its margin (selling price minus purchase price).
slides.narration: Think about the shortcut you have just seen. Does it hold for any selling price above the cost price? Decide, then answer.

slides.heading: Working backwards
slides.body_md: In a **reverse problem** you know the amount paid and must find what came before it. Undo the steps in **reverse order**: the tax first, then the discount.

visual.alt: Table of rules for reverse problems: price before GST is amount times 100 over 100 plus r; rate of GST is the tax over the price times 100; price after discount is the amount divided by 1 plus r over 100; list price is the selling price divided by 1 minus d over 100; rate of discount is the discount over the list price times 100.
visual.caption: Work backwards: undo the tax first, then the discount.

slides.narration: Some problems give you the final amount and ask for something earlier: the price before tax, the rate, the list price or the discount. Undo the steps in reverse order. The tax was added last, so remove it first, by dividing by one plus the rate over one hundred. Then undo the discount. The table lists the rules; each one comes from writing an equation and solving it.

slides.heading: Worked example 4: the price inside an amount
slides.body_md: A family in Mysuru pays ₹11,092 for a washing machine, including GST at 18%. Find the price before GST and the CGST.
bullets: Let the price be ₹$x$: $x + \dfrac{18}{100}x = 11092$, so $1.18x = 11092$

visual.alt: Graph of amount paid against price before GST at 18 percent: a straight line through the origin with slope 1.18. The point (9.4, 11.092) shows a price of 9,400 rupees giving an amount of 11,092 rupees.
visual.caption: Reading back from the amount to the price means dividing by 1.18.

slides.narration: Call the price x. The amount is x plus eighteen percent of x, which is one point one eight x. So one point one eight x equals eleven thousand and ninety two, and x is nine thousand four hundred rupees. Do not take eighteen percent off the amount; that gives the wrong answer because the tax was added to the smaller number. The central tax is nine percent of the price, eight hundred and forty six rupees.

slides.heading: Worked example 5: finding the rate
slides.body_md: A ceiling lamp listed at ₹2,500 is sold at a discount of 8%, and the customer pays ₹2,576. Find the rate of GST.
bullets: Price after discount: $2500 - 200 = 2300$

visual.alt: Table of steps for finding the GST rate on a ceiling lamp: price after an 8 percent discount on 2,500 rupees is 2,300 rupees; GST is 2,576 minus 2,300, which is 276 rupees; the rate is 276 over 2,300 times 100, which is 12 percent.
visual.caption: Always divide the tax by the price before tax.

slides.narration: First find the taxable value: eight percent off two thousand five hundred leaves two thousand three hundred rupees. The tax is the amount paid minus this, two hundred and seventy six rupees. The rate is the tax as a percentage of the price before tax: two hundred and seventy six over two thousand three hundred, times one hundred, which is twelve percent.

slides.heading: Quick check: undo the tax
slides.body_md: A customer pays ₹3,360 for a mattress, including GST at 12%. Find the price before GST.
slides.narration: Undo the tax: what number, increased by twelve percent, gives three thousand three hundred and sixty? Type the price in rupees.

slides.heading: Worked example 6: finding the list price
slides.body_md: After a discount of 16% on the list price and GST at 18% on the reduced price, a customer pays ₹4,956 for a cupboard. Find the list price.
bullets: Selling price $= \dfrac{4956}{1.18} = 4200$
List price $= \dfrac{4200}{0.84} = 5000$
Check: $5000 \times 0.84 \times 1.18 = 4956$

The discount left eighty four percent of the list price, so divide by nought point eight four to get the list price, five thousand rupees. Always check by working forwards again: five thousand, times nought point eight four, times one point one eight, is four thousand nine hundred and fifty six.

slides.heading: Quick check: a retailer in Mangaluru
slides.body_md: A retailer buys a gas stove for ₹6,400 and sells it within the state for ₹7,200 (both before tax). GST is 18%. Find the CGST the retailer pays.

notes.title: Goods and Services Tax (GST) — chapter notes

sections.heading: 1. What GST is
sections.body_md:
The **Goods and Services Tax (GST)** is a single tax on the supply of goods and services in India, in force since 1 July 2017. It replaced many earlier indirect taxes (central excise, VAT, service tax and others).

- It is charged at **every sale** in a supply chain: manufacturer → wholesaler → retailer → consumer.
- It applies to **services** as well as goods (repairs, catering, rent, software).
- The **buyer pays** it, the **seller collects** it and passes it to the government.
- Rates are fixed for each item by the **GST Council** and are revised from time to time. In every problem the rate is **given**; this chapter uses 5%, 12%, 18% and 28%.

key_terms.definition_md: Goods and Services Tax: one tax on the supply of goods and services across India.
The price on which GST is charged: the selling price after any discount, before tax.
The body of the Union and state finance ministers that fixes and revises GST rates.

visual.alt: Flow of a supply chain: manufacturer to wholesaler to retailer to consumer, with GST charged on each sale.
visual.caption: GST is charged at every sale in the chain, not only at the shop counter.

sections.heading: 2. CGST, SGST and IGST
sections.body_md:
Where the seller and the buyer are decides the **heads of tax**:

- **Intra-state** sale (same state): the bill shows **CGST** (central) and **SGST** (state), each at **half** the GST rate.
- **Inter-state** sale (different states): the bill shows **IGST** (integrated) at the **full** rate. The Centre collects it and shares it with the state where the goods are used.

The rate and the total tax are the same in both cases; only the heads differ. (In a union territory without its own legislature, UTGST takes the place of SGST.)

Example: a pump priced ₹15,500 at 18%: Coimbatore to Palakkad, IGST ₹2,790; Coimbatore to Tiruppur, CGST ₹1,395 + SGST ₹1,395.

key_terms.definition_md: Central GST on an intra-state sale, at half the GST rate.
State GST on an intra-state sale, at half the GST rate.
Integrated GST on an inter-state sale, at the full rate.

rows: Nagpur to Pune, both in Maharashtra
CGST + SGST, half the rate each
Centre, which shares it with the state where the goods are used

visual.alt: Table comparing intra-state and inter-state sales: within one state, such as Nagpur to Pune, the bill shows CGST and SGST at half the rate each; between states, such as Coimbatore to Palakkad, it shows IGST at the full rate, collected by the Centre and shared with the destination state.
visual.caption: Where the buyer is decides the heads of tax, not the rate.

visuals.alt: Table of GST rates used in this chapter: 5 percent splits into 2.5 percent CGST and 2.5 percent SGST; 12 percent into 6 and 6; 18 percent into 9 and 9; 28 percent into 14 and 14. For an inter-state sale the whole rate is IGST.
visuals.caption: Within a state the rate is halved; across states it is charged whole as IGST.

sections.heading: 3. The tax invoice
sections.body_md:
A registered seller issues a **tax invoice** showing the taxable value of each item, the rate and amount of CGST and SGST (or IGST), and the invoice value.

With items at **different rates**, tax each line at its own rate, then add:

- School bag ₹1,200 at 12%: GST ₹144
- Calculator ₹850 at 18%: GST ₹153
- Notebooks ₹400 at 5%: GST ₹20

Total GST ₹317; CGST = SGST = ₹158.50; invoice value ₹2,767.

key_terms.definition_md: The bill a registered seller issues, showing taxable value, each tax and the total.
Taxable value plus all the taxes: the amount the buyer pays.

visual.alt: Invoice table of a Bhubaneswar stationery shop: school bag 1,200 rupees at 12 percent, GST 144; scientific calculator 850 rupees at 18 percent, GST 153; pack of notebooks 400 rupees at 5 percent, GST 20. Totals: price 2,450, GST 317, CGST 158.50, SGST 158.50.
visual.caption: Invoice value $= 2450 + 317 = 2767$ rupees.

sections.heading: 4. Discount and GST: what the consumer pays
sections.body_md:
GST is charged on the **selling price after discount**, never on the list price.

1. Discount = d% of the list price; selling price = list price − discount.
2. GST = r% of the selling price.
3. Amount paid = selling price + GST = list price × (1 − d/100) × (1 + r/100).

Example: list price ₹24,000, 15% off, GST 18%: selling price ₹20,400, GST ₹3,672, amount ₹24,072. Note that 15% off and 18% on multiply to 1.003, not 1.03.

key_terms.definition_md: The price printed or quoted before any discount.
The list price minus the discount; it is the taxable value.

formulas.label: List price L, discount d%, GST r%

nodes.label: Plus GST on the selling price

visual.alt: Flow for a discounted sale: list price, minus the discount, gives the selling price, which is the taxable value; GST is added on the selling price to give the amount paid.
visual.caption: Discount first, then tax on what is left.

visuals.alt: Graph of amount paid against list price. The steep line, 1.18 times the list price, is the wrong method of taxing the list price; the lower line, 1.003 times the list price, is the right method of taking 15 percent off and then adding 18 percent GST. At a list price of 24 thousand rupees the lines give 28.32 and 24.072 thousand rupees.
visuals.caption: Taxing the list price would overcharge by more than four thousand rupees here.

sections.heading: 5. Input tax credit and GST with profit or loss
sections.body_md:
A dealer **pays** GST on purchases (**input tax**) and **collects** GST on sales (**output tax**). Through **input tax credit** it pays only the difference:

$$\text{net GST} = \text{output tax} - \text{input tax}.$$

- Within a state, CGST payable = SGST payable = half the net GST.
- At one rate, net GST = r% of (selling price − purchase price): tax on the **value added**.
- **Profit and loss** are worked out on prices **before** tax; the tax is passed on, not earned.
- At a **loss**, output tax < input tax: nothing is payable and the difference stays as credit.

Example: cost ₹5,000, marked 20% up, 10% off, GST 12%: selling price ₹5,400, net GST ₹48 (CGST ₹24 + SGST ₹24), customer pays ₹6,048, profit 8%.

key_terms.definition_md: GST a dealer pays when it buys goods or services for its business.
GST a dealer charges and collects when it sells.
Setting off input tax against output tax, so that only the difference is paid.

nodes.label: GST paid on purchases: input tax
GST collected on sales: output tax
Net GST payable = output tax − input tax

visual.alt: Flow showing input tax credit: the GST a dealer paid on purchases, called input tax, is set off against the GST it collected on sales, called output tax; the dealer pays only the difference.
visual.caption: Input tax credit: pay only the difference.

visuals.alt: Flow for a harmonium: cost 5,000 rupees, marked 20 percent higher at 6,000, sold after a 10 percent discount at 5,400, and the customer pays 6,048 rupees after 12 percent GST.
visuals.caption: Net GST $= 648 - 600 = 48$ rupees.

sections.heading: 6. The supply chain: tax at each stage
sections.body_md:
Make a table: stage, selling price, output tax, input tax, net GST (and CGST, SGST).

- The **first seller** has no input tax and pays the full GST on its price.
- Each later dealer pays output tax minus the previous stage's output tax.
- Adding the payments, the intermediate taxes cancel: **total GST to the government = GST on the final sale**, which the **consumer** bears.

Example (18%, all in Gujarat): sales at ₹3,000, ₹3,600, ₹4,200; payments ₹540, ₹108, ₹108; total ₹756 = 18% of ₹4,200. Without input tax credit the taxes would total ₹1,944 (tax on tax).

**Inter-state link:** the seller charges IGST and sets off its input CGST and SGST: IGST payable = output IGST − input CGST − input SGST. Example: ₹5,520 − ₹4,800 = ₹720.

key_terms.definition_md: The sequence of sales from manufacturer to wholesaler to retailer to consumer.
Tax charged on a price that already includes tax; input tax credit prevents it.

visual.alt: Table of the Gujarat chain at 18 percent: manufacturer sells for 3,000, output tax 540, no input tax, pays 540 as 270 CGST and 270 SGST; wholesaler sells for 3,600, output 648, input 540, pays 108 as 54 and 54; retailer sells for 4,200, output 756, input 648, pays 108 as 54 and 54.
visual.caption: Each row: output tax minus input tax, then halve.

visuals.alt: Bar chart: the manufacturer pays 540 rupees, the wholesaler 108 and the retailer 108; the fourth bar, the consumer tax of 756 rupees, equals the three payments stacked together.
visuals.caption: The first three bars add up to the fourth.

visuals.alt: Table for woollen blankets at 12 percent: the Ludhiana maker sells to a Ludhiana distributor for 40,000 rupees with CGST 2,400 and SGST 2,400; the distributor sells to a Jaipur retailer for 46,000 rupees with IGST 5,520, sets off the 4,800 rupees of input tax and pays 720 rupees of IGST.
visuals.caption: Input CGST and SGST can both be used against output IGST.

sections.heading: 7. Reverse problems
sections.body_md:
Undo the steps in **reverse order**: the tax was added last, so remove it first.

- Price before GST: price = amount × 100/(100 + r). Example: ₹11,092 at 18% → ₹9,400.
- Rate of GST: r = (amount − price)/price × 100. Example: ₹2,300 → ₹2,576 gives 12%.
- List price: list = selling price ÷ (1 − d/100). Example: ₹4,956 after 16% off and 18% GST → selling price ₹4,200 → list ₹5,000.
- Rate of discount: d = (list − selling price)/list × 100.
- From a dealer's payment at one rate: its margin = payment × 100/r.

Never take r% **off** the amount: 82% of ₹1,180 is ₹967.60, but the price is ₹1,000.

key_terms.definition_md: A problem that gives the final amount and asks for an earlier quantity: price, rate, list price or discount.

visual.alt: Table of rules for reverse problems: price before GST is amount times 100 over 100 plus r; rate of GST is the tax over the price times 100; price after discount is the amount divided by 1 plus r over 100; list price is the selling price divided by 1 minus d over 100; rate of discount is the discount over the list price times 100.
visual.caption: Work backwards: undo the tax first, then the discount.

visuals.alt: Graph of amount paid against price before GST at 18 percent: a straight line through the origin with slope 1.18. The point (9.4, 11.092) shows a price of 9,400 rupees giving an amount of 11,092 rupees.
visuals.caption: Reading back from the amount to the price means dividing by 1.18.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**How marks are awarded**
- *GST on a bill (2–3 marks):* GST on each item (1), CGST and SGST or IGST correctly chosen and split (1), invoice value (1).
- *Discount and GST (3 marks):* selling price after discount (1), GST on the selling price (1), amount paid (1).
- *Supply chain (4 marks in Section A, or a 3 + 3 + 4 structured question):* selling price at each stage (1), output and input tax (1), net GST of each dealer (1), CGST/SGST split or the total equal to the consumer's tax (1).
- *Reverse problems (3–4 marks):* equation such as $1.18x = \text{amount}$ (1), price (1), then rate, list price or discount (1–2).

**Common mistakes**
1. Charging GST on the list price instead of the price after discount.
2. Using IGST for a sale within a state, or CGST and SGST for a sale between states.
3. Writing CGST at the full rate instead of half.
4. Forgetting that the first seller in a chain has no input tax.
5. Adding the output taxes of all stages to get the government's total.
6. Working out profit on prices that include GST.
7. Taking r% off the amount paid to remove the tax (divide by 1 + r/100 instead).
8. Rounding paise: ₹158.50 is exact, not ₹159.

cards.front_md: What does GST stand for, and since when has it been in force?
cards.back_md: Goods and Services Tax; since 1 July 2017.

cards.front_md: Formula for GST at r% on a price?
cards.back_md: $\text{GST} = \dfrac{r}{100} \times \text{price}$

cards.front_md: Intra-state sale: how is GST shown on the bill?
cards.back_md: CGST and SGST, each at half the rate.

cards.front_md: Inter-state sale: how is GST shown on the bill?
cards.back_md: IGST at the full rate.

cards.front_md: GST 18% within a state: CGST and SGST rates?
cards.back_md: 9% each.

cards.front_md: GST 5% within a state: CGST and SGST rates?
cards.back_md: 2.5% each.

cards.front_md: Who fixes GST rates?
cards.back_md: The GST Council (Union and state finance ministers); rates are revised from time to time.

cards.front_md: Does the total tax change between an intra-state and an inter-state sale at the same rate?
cards.back_md: No: only the heads (CGST + SGST or IGST) change.

cards.front_md: Bill with items at different rates: method?
cards.back_md: Tax each line at its own rate, then add.

cards.front_md: Picture: a table with two rows, same state and different states. What does it show?
cards.back_md: Same state → CGST + SGST at half rates; different states → IGST at the full rate.

cards.front_md: On which price is GST charged when a discount is given?
cards.back_md: The selling price after the discount.

cards.front_md: Amount paid from list price L, discount d%, GST r%?
cards.back_md: $L\left(1 - \dfrac{d}{100}\right)\left(1 + \dfrac{r}{100}\right)$

cards.front_md: 15% off, then 18% GST: overall multiplier?
Does x% off then x% tax bring the price back to the list price?
cards.back_md: No: it gives (1 − x²/10000) times the list price, slightly less.

cards.front_md: Taxable value means?
cards.back_md: The price after any discount, before tax.

cards.front_md: Input tax?
cards.back_md: GST a dealer pays on its purchases.

cards.front_md: Output tax?
cards.back_md: GST a dealer collects on its sales.

cards.front_md: Net GST payable by a dealer?
cards.back_md: Output tax − input tax (input tax credit).

cards.front_md: Same rate r% on buying and selling: net GST?
cards.back_md: r% of (selling price − purchase price).

cards.front_md: Input tax of the first seller in a chain?
cards.back_md: Zero: it pays the full GST on its price.

cards.front_md: Total GST received by the government along a chain (one rate)?
cards.back_md: The GST on the final sale, borne by the consumer.

cards.front_md: Can a consumer claim input tax credit?
cards.back_md: No: the consumer is at the end of the chain and bears the tax.

cards.front_md: Profit percent with GST: on which prices?
cards.back_md: Prices before tax; GST is passed on, not earned.

cards.front_md: Dealer sells at a loss (same rate): net GST?
cards.back_md: Negative: nothing payable; the difference stays as credit.

cards.front_md: Inter-state sale after an intra-state purchase: IGST payable?
cards.back_md: Output IGST − input CGST − input SGST.

cards.front_md: Picture: four bars, three small payments and one tall bar. What does it show?
cards.back_md: The dealers’ payments add up to the consumer’s tax.

cards.front_md: Mixer-grinder chain at 18%: sales ₹3,000, ₹3,600, ₹4,200. Payments?
Price before GST from an amount A at r%?
cards.back_md: $A \times \dfrac{100}{100 + r}$

cards.front_md: Rate of GST from price P and amount A?
cards.back_md: $\dfrac{A - P}{P} \times 100$

cards.front_md: ₹11,092 including 18% GST: price?
Reverse problem with a discount and GST: order of undoing?
cards.back_md: Undo the tax first (÷ 1 + r/100), then the discount (÷ 1 − d/100).

cards.back_md: The 18% was added to the smaller price; 82% of ₹1,180 is ₹967.60, not ₹1,000.

questions.stem_md: Under GST, when a dealer sells goods to a buyer in the same state, the tax charged on the bill is

options.text_md: CGST and SGST, in equal parts
IGST only
CGST only
SGST only

questions.solution_md: An intra-state supply is taxed by both governments: half the rate as central GST and half as state GST. IGST, option (b), is for supplies from one state to another.

questions.stem_md: A geyser is sold by a shop in Shimla to a family in Shimla at a GST rate of 12%. The rate of central GST on the bill is
questions.solution_md: Intra-state: the $12\%$ is shared equally, so CGST is charged at $6\%$ and SGST at $6\%$. Option (c) is the full GST rate.

questions.stem_md: A handicraft store in Shillong sells a cane chair for ₹2,350 to a buyer in Shillong. GST is charged at 12%. The SGST on the bill is
questions.solution_md: GST $= \dfrac{12}{100} \times 2350 = 282$; SGST is half of it, ₹141. Option (d) is the whole GST, and option (b) wrongly adds only the SGST to the price.

questions.stem_md: A tea trader in Guwahati (Assam) sends tea packets priced at ₹18,600 to a buyer in Siliguri (West Bengal). GST is 5%. The tax on the invoice is

options.text_md: CGST of ₹465 and SGST of ₹465
IGST of ₹465
CGST of ₹930 and SGST of ₹930
IGST of ₹930

questions.solution_md: Assam to West Bengal is an inter-state supply, so the full $5\%$ is charged as IGST: $\dfrac{5}{100} \times 18600 = 930$. Option (a) would be right only for a sale inside Assam.

questions.stem_md: A kitchenware shop in Mysuru bills a local customer for a pressure cooker at ₹1,850 (GST 12%) and an electric kettle at ₹1,250 (GST 18%). The total GST on the bill is
questions.solution_md: Tax each line at its own rate: $\dfrac{12}{100} \times 1850 = 222$ and $\dfrac{18}{100} \times 1250 = 225$, total ₹447. Options (b) and (c) use one rate for both items; option (d) is the whole bill.

questions.stem_md: An almirah has a list price of ₹5,600. The shop gives a discount of 10% and then charges GST at 18%. The GST charged is
questions.solution_md: GST is charged on the reduced price: $5600 - 560 = 5040$, and $\dfrac{18}{100} \times 5040 = 907.20$. Option (c) taxes the list price; option (a) is the amount paid.

questions.stem_md: A split air conditioner listed at ₹12,500 is sold at a discount of 20%, and GST at 28% is added to the reduced price. The customer pays
questions.solution_md: Reduced price ₹10,000; GST $= \dfrac{28}{100} \times 10000 = 2800$; amount ₹12,800. Option (d) treats it as "$8\%$ more than the list price", option (a) ignores the discount and option (b) ignores the tax.

questions.stem_md: When a shopkeeper gives a discount on the list price of an article and then charges GST, the GST is calculated on

options.text_md: the list price
the discount
the price the shopkeeper paid for the article
the price after the discount

questions.solution_md: Tax is charged on the value of the sale, which is the price the buyer actually agrees to pay before tax: the list price minus the discount.

questions.stem_md: Input tax credit under GST allows a registered dealer to

options.text_md: deduct the GST paid on purchases from the GST collected on sales
add the GST paid on purchases to the selling price
avoid charging GST to the next buyer
collect GST twice on the same article

questions.solution_md: The dealer pays the government only the difference: GST collected on sales (output tax) minus GST already paid on purchases (input tax).

questions.stem_md: In one month a dealer in Ranchi collected GST of ₹1,440 on sales and had paid GST of ₹1,080 on purchases of the same goods. The net GST the dealer pays to the government is
questions.solution_md: Net GST $= 1440 - 1080 = 360$. Option (c) adds instead of subtracting; option (d) is only the central half of the net amount.

questions.stem_md: A wholesaler in Kanpur buys a consignment of school bags for ₹8,000 and sells it to a retailer in Lucknow (both in Uttar Pradesh) for ₹9,500. GST is 12%. The CGST paid by the wholesaler to the government is
questions.solution_md: Output CGST $= 6\% \text{ of } 9500 = 570$; input CGST $= 6\% \text{ of } 8000 = 480$; CGST payable $= 570 - 480 = 90$. Option (d) is the total net GST, and option (a) forgets the input credit.

questions.stem_md: Solar lanterns pass from a manufacturer to a wholesaler for ₹24,000, from the wholesaler to a retailer for ₹27,600, and from the retailer to a consumer for ₹31,200, all within Odisha. GST is 5% at every stage. The total GST received by the government is
questions.solution_md: The net payments are $1200 + 180 + 180 = 1560$, which is $5\%$ of the final price $31200$. Option (a) adds every output tax and so counts the same tax again and again.

questions.stem_md: Goods pass from a manufacturer through a wholesaler and a retailer to a consumer, all in one state, at a single GST rate, and every dealer sells for more than it paid. The total GST received by the government equals

options.text_md: the GST paid by the consumer on the final price
the sum of the GST charged at every sale
the GST on the price charged by the manufacturer
zero, because every dealer claims input tax credit

questions.solution_md: Each dealer pays output tax minus input tax, so when the payments are added the intermediate taxes cancel and only the tax on the last sale is left. That tax is borne by the consumer.

questions.stem_md: A dealer in Jammu buys a sewing machine for ₹4,000 (before GST) and sells it to a customer in Jammu at a profit of 15%. GST is 18% on both sales. The net GST the dealer pays to the government is
questions.solution_md: Selling price $= 4600$. Output tax $= 828$, input tax $= 720$, net $= 108$, which is $18\%$ of the profit ₹600. Option (a) is only the CGST part.

questions.stem_md: A customer in Bhopal pays ₹2,124 for a set of bedsheets, including GST at 18%. The price of the bedsheets before GST is
questions.solution_md: Price $= 2124 \times \dfrac{100}{118} = 1800$. Option (d) takes $18\%$ off the amount paid, which is wrong because the $18\%$ was added to the smaller price.

questions.stem_md: After a discount, a study lamp is priced at ₹3,750. A customer pays ₹4,200 including GST. The rate of GST is
questions.solution_md: GST $= 4200 - 3750 = 450$, and rate $= \dfrac{450}{3750} \times 100 = 12$ percent. Divide by the price before tax, not by the amount paid.

questions.stem_md: A customer pays ₹6,608 for a pair of running shoes after a discount of 20% on the list price and GST at 18% on the reduced price. The list price is

An office printer passes from a manufacturer to a wholesaler, to a retailer and then to a customer, all within Odisha. GST is 18% at every sale. The GST paid to the government is ₹1,350 by the manufacturer, ₹270 by the wholesaler and ₹324 by the retailer.

(a) Find the price at which the manufacturer sold the printer. [3]

(b) Find the prices at which the wholesaler and the retailer sold it. [3]

(c) Find the amount the customer pays, and verify that the total GST received by the government equals the GST paid by the customer. [4]

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** The manufacturer has no input tax, so its payment is $18\%$ of its price: price $= 1350 \times \dfrac{100}{18} = 7500$.

**(b)** The wholesaler pays $18\%$ of its margin: margin $= 270 \times \dfrac{100}{18} = 1500$, so its price $= 7500 + 1500 = 9000$.

Retailer's margin $= 324 \times \dfrac{100}{18} = 1800$, so its price $= 10800$.

**(c)** GST on the final sale $= \dfrac{18}{100} \times 10800 = 1944$; the customer pays $10800 + 1944 = 12744$.

Total received $= 1350 + 270 + 324 = 1944$, the same as the customer's GST.
